title: Where Am I?
brief: First rule on the bench: before you touch any evidence, put your position on the record. Print the full path of the directory you are standing in. That line is the first entry in your case log.

hints.text: The command is `pwd` — print working directory. Type it and press Enter.

successMessage: You are at /home/examiner. `pwd` always prints your absolute position in the directory tree, whatever the prompt happens to be showing.

title: Survey the Bench
brief: You cannot examine what you have not inventoried. Find out what this workstation was handed to you with: show the files and directories in the place you are standing.

hints.text: The command is `ls` — list. On its own it lists wherever you currently are.

successMessage: `ls` lists directory contents. The bench came with Documents, evidence, training, and welcome.txt — and, as you are about to find out, more than that.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight
brief: The examiner who had this bench before you left something behind, and a plain `ls` does not show it. On Linux, a filename that starts with a dot is invisible to a normal listing. Find the hidden file in your home directory, read it, and submit the find inside.

hints.text: `ls -a` lists everything, dotfiles included.
The file is called `.stash`. Read it with `cat .stash` and submit the recovered find.

successMessage: Dotfiles like `.bashrc` and `.stash` are hidden by default, which is exactly why intruders like them. `ls -a` is the habit worth keeping.

title: One Level Down
brief: Your onboarding folder recorded a checkpoint for you. Get inside `training/level_1`, read `checkpoint_alpha.txt`, and submit the find it holds.

hints.text: Use `cd training/level_1` to move down into it.
Once inside level_1, run `cat checkpoint_alpha.txt` to see the find.

successMessage: `cd` changes your working directory. You walked down through `training` into `level_1` in one move.

title: Sideways Move
brief: Now reach `training/level_2` — a SIBLING of level_1, not a child. If you are standing inside level_1, you have to go up before you can go over. Read `checkpoint_beta.txt` and submit the find.

hints.text: A sibling directory is reached by going UP first, then over. From your home directory the whole trip is one command: `cd training/level_2`.
Once you are inside, run `cat checkpoint_beta.txt` and submit the find.

successMessage: `..` means the parent directory. `cd ..` moves you one level up, toward the root.
commandCheckExemptReason: Hint is conditional on already being inside level_1; the absolute-path alternative is verified instead.

title: Warp Speed (Tab Completion)
brief: Typing full paths is slow, and a typo in a path is how the wrong file ends up in a report. Get yourself into your `Documents` directory without typing the whole name — make the shell finish it for you.

hints.text: Type `cd Doc`, press the Tab key — the shell completes it to `cd Documents` — then press Enter.

successMessage: Tab completion prevents typos and saves keystrokes. On a real case it is the difference between reading the exhibit you meant and the one next to it.
commandCheckExemptReason: Intentionally incomplete prefix — the challenge is to press Tab to complete it.

title: Recall the Past (History)
brief: Examiners repeat commands constantly, and retyping is how mistakes creep in. Bring back a command you have already run — the one that printed your position — and run it again without typing it out.

hints.text: Press the Up Arrow key to walk back through your command history until you reach `pwd`, then press Enter.

successMessage: Up and Down arrows cycle through your command history. With Tab completion, that is most of what fast terminal work actually is.

title: Read the Case File
brief: Nothing else in this act makes sense until you have read the case file end to end. Put the whole of `Documents/case_1042.txt` on screen: the top says what Aurora Robotics reported, the bottom says what this lab expects of you.

hints.text: One command prints a whole file to the screen. It is called `cat`, short for concatenate.
Run `cat Documents/case_1042.txt`.

successMessage: `cat` prints a file in full. Any command that put the whole file on screen counts here — the check looked at what appeared, not at what you typed.

title: The Night Shift
brief: `Documents/access.log` is the workstation timeline recovered from the seized laptop. Its first five entries alone show the machine being opened twice: once in daylight, and once at an hour when nobody was meant to be in the building. Put exactly those first five entries on screen.

success.text:
2026-03-14 08:02:11 - SESSION: workstation unlocked by badge 4417, day shift
2026-03-14 08:04:56 - SHARE: mounted //aurora-fs/prototypes read-only
2026-03-14 17:40:03 - SESSION: workstation locked, badge 4417 signed out
2026-03-15 02:14:39 - SESSION: workstation unlocked by badge 4417, OUT OF HOURS
2026-03-15 02:15:02 - SHARE: remounted //aurora-fs/prototypes read-write

hints.text: `head` prints the top of a file. One find says how many lines you want.
Run `head -n 5 Documents/access.log`.

successMessage: `head` shows the start of a file — ten lines by default, five with `-n 5`. That 02:14 unlock is the first real lead in Case 1042.

title: The Last Record
brief: A timeline is only as good as its ends. You have read the beginning; the final record is the one the intake sheet refers to, written when the laptop reached this lab. Read the end of `Documents/access.log` and submit the find on the last line.

hints.text: `tail` prints the bottom of a file — the opposite end from `head`.
Run `tail Documents/access.log`, then submit the find on the final line.

successMessage: `tail` shows the final lines of a file. On a live machine `tail -f` keeps printing as new lines arrive, which is how incidents are watched in real time.

title: Don't Trust the Name
brief: Exhibit `evidence/mystery_file` arrived with its extension stripped off. An examiner never identifies a file by its name — the answer is in the first few bytes of the file itself. Work out what this exhibit really is.

hints.text: One command reads a file's magic bytes and reports what it truly is.
Run `file evidence/mystery_file`.

successMessage: `file` reads the signature at the start of the file — the magic bytes — and ignores the name completely. It is a PNG image, whatever it was called.

title: Carving Text Out of a Binary
brief: `evidence/binary_data` is a compiled program, so `cat` gives you screenfuls of garbage. Pull the readable text out of it instead, and submit the recovery token hidden among the strings.

hints.text: One command extracts printable character sequences from a binary.
Run `strings evidence/binary_data`, then submit the recovery token in the output.

successMessage: `strings` pulls runs of four or more printable characters out of binaries, memory dumps, and damaged files. It is the first move in almost every malware triage.

title: Integrity Checksum (MD5)
brief: Evidence has to be hashed so the lab can prove nobody altered it — before examination and after. Compute the MD5 hash of `evidence/evidence.img`, then read the image header and submit the acquisition find recorded there.

hints.text: One command computes an MD5 digest. Reading the header afterwards is an ordinary `cat`.
Run `md5sum evidence/evidence.img`, then `cat evidence/evidence.img`.

successMessage: Hash on acquisition, hash again afterwards, and the two matching numbers are your proof the image was never touched. That record is the chain of custody.

title: Secrets in Plain Sight
brief: `Documents/secrets.txt` came off the seized laptop and only one line of it matters to this case. Find the line that carries `vault_passcode` and submit the find on it.

hints.text: `grep` searches a file for a pattern. Give it the pattern first, then the file.
Run `grep vault_passcode Documents/secrets.txt`.

successMessage: `grep` finds matching lines in a file. It is the single most used tool in this whole trade.

title: Case-Insensitive Searching
brief: `Documents/logs.txt` records failures inconsistently: some lines say 'error', some 'ERROR'. A search that only matches one of them misses evidence. Find every error line with a single search, then submit the find one of them carries.

hints.text: One short `grep` find makes the match ignore letter case.
Run `grep -i "error" Documents/logs.txt`.

successMessage: `grep -i` ignores case. Real logs are written by many programs with no agreement about capitals, so this find is not a convenience — it is the difference between finding evidence and missing it.

title: Needle in /var/log
brief: Aurora's badge readers write to this machine, somewhere under `/var/log`, and you do not know the filename. List every file under `/var/log` whose name ends in `.log`, then read the badge audit and submit the code recorded when badge 4417 was accepted at 02:14.

hints.text: `find` walks a whole directory tree and can filter on the filename. Quote the wildcard pattern so the shell leaves it alone.
Run `find /var/log -name "*.log"`, then `cat /var/log/badge_audit.log`.

successMessage: `find` searches an entire hierarchy by name, type, size, or timestamp. The badge reader puts your suspect at the engineering floor door one minute before the workstation was unlocked.

title: The WSL Bridge
brief: This bench runs Linux, but the seized laptop's Windows filesystem is mounted alongside it at `/mnt/c`. Read the evidence intake sheet at `/mnt/c/Users/Examiner/Desktop/CASE_FILES/intake.txt` and submit the verification find on it.

hints.text: WSL mounts each Windows drive under `/mnt`, so drive C: shows up as `/mnt/c`.
Run `cat /mnt/c/Users/Examiner/Desktop/CASE_FILES/intake.txt`.

successMessage: That is the WSL bridge: `C:\Users\x` on the Windows side is `/mnt/c/Users/x` from Linux. One machine, two views of the same disk.

title: The Bridge, Unassisted
brief: The examiner before you left handover notes on the Windows side, at `C:\Users\Examiner\Documents\handover_notes.txt`. Reach them from this Linux shell and submit the bridge token inside. Nobody is going to translate the path for you this time.

hints.text: Translate the Windows path yourself: `C:\` becomes `/mnt/c/`, and every backslash becomes a forward slash.
Run `cat /mnt/c/Users/Examiner/Documents/handover_notes.txt`.

successMessage: You converted a Windows path into its WSL location without a map. That is a skill every mixed Windows-and-Linux lab needs.

title: Consult the Manual
brief: The bench tool `evtrace` has a manual override code, and it is written down in exactly one place: the tool's own manual page. Read the manual, find the code, and submit it.

hints.text: Every serious Linux tool ships a manual page, and one command opens it.
Run `man evtrace` and read the DESCRIPTION section.

successMessage: `man` opens the manual page that ships with a tool. Reading the manual before asking is the whole difference between guessing at a tool and using it.

title: Install the Bench Tool (apt-get)
brief: `evtrace` is not installed on this workstation yet. Install it from the package repository, then replay every recorded source and submit the code the badge reader stream prints.

hints.text: Refresh the package lists first, then install. Both steps need administrator rights. The replay-everything find for `evtrace` is `-a`.
Run `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install evtrace -y`, then `evtrace -a`.

successMessage: `apt-get` is how Debian and Ubuntu machines fetch software. `update` refreshes the catalogue, `install` fetches the package, and `sudo` supplies the rights for both.

title: Filter the Noise (Inverted Grep)
brief: `Documents/network_stream.log` is almost all ordinary allowed traffic, and the one line that matters is buried in it. Show only the packets that were NOT allowed, then submit the find on the CRITICAL_DATA_LEAK entry.

hints.text: `grep` normally keeps the lines that match. One find inverts that and keeps everything else.
Run `grep -v "ALLOW" Documents/network_stream.log`.

successMessage: `grep -v` inverts the match. Removing the normal traffic is usually faster than describing the abnormal traffic you are looking for.

title: First Pipeline (grep | wc -l)
brief: Your report needs a number, not a listing: how many packets in `Documents/network_stream.log` were not allowed? Get that count onto the screen and nothing else. A pipeline is the classic way to do it, but this challenge grades the number you produced, so any command that prints the right count scores.

hints.text: The `|` operator feeds one command's output straight into the next, and `wc -l` counts lines.
Run `grep -v "ALLOW" Documents/network_stream.log | wc -l`. The shorter `grep -vc ALLOW Documents/network_stream.log` reaches the same number and is accepted too.

successMessage: Nine packets were not allowed. The pipe `|` sent grep's output into `wc -l` — and `grep -vc` does the whole job in one process. Both are correct, because the count was what the case asked for.

title: Extracting Fields (cut and grep)
brief: `Documents/security_events.csv` is comma separated, and the rows tagged `FLAG_EMIT` carry a token in column 6. Isolate those rows, cut out just that column, and submit the token.

hints.text: Two commands joined by a pipe: `grep` picks the rows, `cut` picks the column. `cut` needs to be told the delimiter and the field number.
Run `grep "FLAG_EMIT" Documents/security_events.csv | cut -d, -f6`.

successMessage: `grep` for rows, `cut -d, -f<N>` for columns. Between them you can slice a structured log apart without ever opening a spreadsheet.

title: Output Redirection (>)
brief: Findings that only exist on screen are not findings. Pull every error line out of `Documents/logs.txt` — however it is capitalised — and save them to a new file at `/tmp/errors.log` instead of printing them. Then read that file back to confirm the capture worked.

hints.text: `>` sends output into a file instead of the screen. Do not forget the find that makes the search ignore case, or you will miss lines.
Run `grep -i "error" Documents/logs.txt > /tmp/errors.log`, then `cat /tmp/errors.log`.

successMessage: `>` writes standard output straight into a file. Seven error lines are now saved where a report can cite them.

title: Partition Geometry Inspection
brief: `evidence/seized_drive.raw` is the raw image of the drive that left the building. Somewhere in it is an encrypted container, and you cannot carve it out until you know which sector it starts at. Read the image's partition table with the bench tool `scan`, and write the container's start offset down — the next challenge asks for it.

hints.text: `scan` takes the path to the image and nothing else.
Run `scan evidence/seized_drive.raw` and read the Start Sector Offset it reports for partition 2.

successMessage: The partition table puts partition 2 — the encrypted container — at sector offset 206848. Keep that number where you can find it.

title: Carve the Container (Finish Line)
brief: This is the whole case in one exercise. `evidence/seized_drive.raw` hides an encrypted container, and the prototype files walked out inside it. The bench tool `extract` can carve that container, but only if you hand it the exact sector offset where the container begins — and it refuses a wrong one. You recovered that number from the partition table; go back for it if you did not write it down. Carve the container and submit the case find it gives up.

hints.text: `extract` takes the offset with the `-o` find, then the image path. The offset came out of the `scan` output, and the tool will reject anything else.
Run `extract -o 206848 evidence/seized_drive.raw`, then submit the case find it prints.

successMessage: You read partition geometry, carried a number from one tool's output into another tool's argument, and carved out the container. That chain is what forensic work actually looks like. Case 1042 is closed.

title: Windows Navigation (dir and cd)
brief: You are now working the seized laptop from its own Windows command line. Start the same way you started on Linux: show what is in `C:\Users\Examiner`.

hints.text: In cmd.exe the listing command is `dir`. Typed on its own, `cd` prints where you are instead of moving you.
Run `dir`.

successMessage: `dir` is the Windows counterpart of `ls`. Note the backslashes: Windows separates path components with `\`, Linux with `/`.

title: Hidden File Attributes (attrib)
brief: Windows hides a file with an attribute bit, not with a leading dot, so the Linux trick you learned in Act I will not find it here. Inspect the attributes of `evidence\mystery_file`, then read it and recover the find.

hints.text: `attrib` shows a file's attribute letters, and H means Hidden. `type` prints a file the way `cat` does on Linux.
Run `attrib evidence\mystery_file`, then `type evidence\mystery_file`.

successMessage: `attrib` shows and changes file attributes: R read-only, H hidden, S system, A archive. Same idea as a dotfile, different mechanism.

title: Windows String Search (findstr /i)
brief: The laptop's event log extract is at `Documents\logs.txt`. Find the evidence marker in it, ignoring letter case, and submit the find. There is no `grep` on Windows.

hints.text: The cmd.exe search command is `findstr`. Its switches start with a forward slash, and `/i` ignores case.
Run `findstr /i "marker" Documents\logs.txt`.

successMessage: `findstr /i` is the Windows answer to `grep -i`. Different name, same job: keep the lines that match.

title: CertUtil Hashing
brief: Finish the chain of custody on the Windows side: compute the MD5 hash of `evidence\evidence.img`. Windows ships no `md5sum`, so use the tool that is already on every Windows machine.

hints.text: `certutil` needs the `-hashfile` switch, then the file, then the name of the algorithm.
Run `certutil -hashfile evidence\evidence.img MD5`.

successMessage: `certutil -hashfile` computes MD5, SHA1, or SHA256 with nothing installed. Every Windows workstation can hash evidence out of the box.
